# Reflection — Morgen-Lite

> **Note:** This feedback is AI-generated and experimental. It's meant to surface useful observations, not to grade you. Take what resonates, ignore what doesn't. Your own sense of what you learned matters more than anything here.

## Scope & Idea Clarity

**What went well:** The scope doc nails the idea in one sentence — "A blazingly fast, local-first personal calendar and task manager." The user is specific ("me — a full stack engineer"), cuts are real with rationale (no Google Calendar integration because "huge time sink"), and the one deepening round produced the key insight: "Performance is the #1 win condition." That single sentence shaped every technical decision that followed.

**What to try next time:** Push "What Done Looks Like" to include measurable targets. "Virtual scrolling for performance" is good, but adding a metric (e.g., "scrolls smoothly with 500+ events") makes verification concrete during the build.

## Requirements Thinking

**What went well:** The PRD delivers 4 epics / 12 stories / ~40 acceptance criteria — exactly what you'd write for a real project. Criteria like "Grid displays all 24 hours (0:00–23:59) on the vertical axis" leave zero ambiguity for the builder. The "What We're Building" vs "What We'd Add" section shows genuine prioritization thinking, and the open questions surfaced during /prd (calendar library, grid resolution, edit interface) were all resolved in the spec.

**What to try next time:** You skipped all deepening rounds in /prd, going straight to document generation. Those rounds are where edge cases surface — "what happens if I drop a todo on an occupied time slot?" or "what if there are 100+ events?" Next time, invest in at least one deepening round to stress-test the requirements before moving to spec.

## Technical Decisions

**What went well:** The spec shows intentional architecture at senior-dev level. The trud-calendar choice is well-reasoned (MIT license, TypeScript-native, built-in drag-drop/resize, shadcn theming), and you explicitly called out the tradeoff: "very new library (v0.1.4, 0 GitHub stars) — smaller community, potential undiscovered bugs." The data flow diagram, file structure with annotations, and PRD cross-references show you know exactly how everything connects.

**What to try next time:** The checklist sequencing is logical, but all 9 items were built autonomously without checkpoints. As someone who wants to learn steering techniques, try a hybrid approach: plan autonomously, then switch to guided mode for 1-2 complex items (like the drag-to-schedule logic). That's where you'd practice course-correcting the agent in real time.

## Plan vs. Reality

**What went well:** The build matched the plan closely. All 9 checklist items completed successfully. The split layout, three views, drag-to-schedule, click-to-create, event resize/drag/edit/delete, dark theme with neon accents, and Dexie persistence — it all landed. The trud-calendar bugs encountered (`useCalendarContext` issue, TypeScript mismatches) were worked around without changing the plan.

**What to try next time:** The `create-next-app` scaffolding failed initially due to `process-notes.md` in the root — a small thing, but the plan didn't account for existing files in the project directory. A pre-build environment check in checklist item 1 would prevent that. Also, the spec called for "subtle circuit board textures" — a quick reality check during the polish step would confirm it landed as intended.

## How You Worked

**What went well:** You were decisive and knew exactly what you wanted. Process notes show a consistent pattern: "That's perfect", "Looks good", "ready to proceed" — you moved fast without getting bogged down. You actively chose autonomous build mode because you wanted to "review final result rather than checkpoint," a deliberate choice aligned with your learning goal. Your one deepening round in /scope produced the performance-first priority that shaped everything.

**What to try next time:** You acknowledged wanting to "spend even more time on the plan and doing deeper dives." Process notes show 0 deepening rounds in /prd, /spec, and /checklist. For learning steering techniques specifically, the real practice happens *during* the build, not just before it. Next time, try guided mode for at least part of the build so you can practice redirecting the agent when it goes off-track.

## Your Goals

At the start, you said you wanted to **walk away knowing how to prompt and steer coding agents more effectively**.

You made real progress on this, but in an unexpected way — you discovered that the real "prompting" happens before you write a single line of code. The autonomous build worked because the planning docs were thorough, giving the agent everything it needed. What you didn't get to practice was the *mid-build steering* — redirecting, course-correcting, and shaping the code as it's being written. That's the other half of steering. The planning piece? You nailed it. The mid-build piece? That's what to explore next.

## Reflection

**What surprised you most?** "How little time the planning actually took! But it was worth it." This is the core insight of spec-driven development — thorough planning is fast when you know what you want, and it pays for itself many times over during the build.
